==Problem 15==
Let the letters <imath>F</imath>,<imath>L</imath>,<imath>Y</imath>,<imath>B</imath>,<imath>U</imath>,<imath>G</imath> represent distinct digits. Suppose <imath>\underline{F}~\underline{L}~\underline{Y}~\underline{F}~\underline{L}~\underline{Y}</imath> is the greatest number that satisfies the equation

<cmath>8\cdot\underline{F}~\underline{L}~\underline{Y}~\underline{F}~\underline{L}~\underline{Y}=\underline{B}~\underline{U}~\underline{G}~\underline{B}~\underline{U}~\underline{G}.</cmath>

What is the value of <imath>\underline{F}~\underline{L}~\underline{Y}+\underline{B}~\underline{U}~\underline{G}</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 1089 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 1098 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 1107 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 1116 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 1125</imath>

==Solution 1==
Let <imath>\overline{FLY}</imath> be the <imath>3</imath>-digit number <imath>100F+10L+Y</imath>.

Repeating a <imath>3</imath>-digit block twice gives
<cmath>
\overline{FLYFLY}=1000\cdot \overline{FLY}+\overline{FLY}=1001\cdot \overline{FLY}.
</cmath>
Similarly,
<cmath>
\overline{BUGBUG}=1001\cdot \overline{BUG}.
</cmath>

Given <imath>8\cdot \overline{FLYFLY}=\overline{BUGBUG}</imath>, substitute:
<cmath>
8(1001\overline{FLY})=1001\overline{BUG}.
</cmath>
Divide by <imath>1001</imath>:
<cmath>
8\overline{FLY}=\overline{BUG}.
</cmath>

Since <imath>\overline{BUG}</imath> is a <imath>3</imath>-digit number,
<cmath>
100\le 8\overline{FLY}\le 999
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
13\le \overline{FLY}\le 124.
</cmath>
To maximize <imath>\overline{FLYFLY}</imath>, maximize <imath>\overline{FLY}</imath>.

Try the largest possible value:
<cmath>
\overline{FLY}=123
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\overline{BUG}=8\cdot 123=984.
</cmath>
The digits <imath>\{1,2,3,9,8,4\}</imath> are all distinct, so this works and is maximal.

Therefore,
<cmath>
\overline{FLY}+\overline{BUG}=123+984=1107.
</cmath>

<cmath>
\boxed{1107}
</cmath>

~ Shreyan of Winston Churchill Middle School

==Solution 2==
The divisibility rule for <imath>8</imath> is that the last <imath>3</imath> digits need to be divisible by <imath>8</imath>. That means that <imath>BUG</imath> needs to be a multiple of <imath>8</imath> with distinct digits. And since multiplying <imath>8</imath> by <imath>FLY</imath> gives <imath>BUG</imath>, we know that the number needs to be a product of <imath>8</imath> and a <imath>3</imath> digit number. From the more foundational multiplication facts, we know that <imath>125\cdot 8 = 1000</imath>. Moving down from there, we can try <imath>124 * 8 = 992</imath>. This won't work because <imath>992</imath> does not have distinct digits. Next, we can try <imath>123 * 8 = 984</imath>. <imath>1, 2, 3, 9, 8,</imath> and <imath>4</imath> are all distinct digits. That means that <imath>FLY = 123</imath> and <imath>BUG = 984</imath>. <imath>123 + 984 = 1107</imath>, so the answer is <imath>\boxed C</imath>. Note that while guessing and checking multiples of <imath>8</imath> sounds like an unreliable strategy, we know that the number needs to be <imath>8\cdot FLYFLY</imath>, which would for certain be a large number. 

-mathdragonmochi
